title: First wheeled vehicle runs on the French Damascus road
why: Jessup says the first wheeled vehicle in Syria ran in 1861 on the French diligence road; a carriage branch to Baabda followed about 1865.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 117; see Cuinet 1896, p. 41
note: Existing record dates the road opening to 1863 (Cuinet: begun 1850, in service 1863). Jessup p. 265 shows the road company in Beirut in Feb 1863.

title: Al-Jawa'ib founded in Constantinople by Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq
why: The Arabic paper, edited by the Lebanese-born writer, ran until 1884 and became widely read in Beirut literary circles.
note: Published in Istanbul, not Lebanon; included as a Lebanese-edited Arabic paper.

title: Beirut Native Protestant Female Seminary opens with six charity pupils
why: Jessup says no parent would pay a piastre for a daughter's schooling in 1861; he carried the school on his own appeals for nine years.

title: Christian refugees from the 1860 war leave for Egypt
why: Hitti says the Druze-Christian fighting drove many Christians to Egypt, the first step for some on the road to the Americas.

title: Druze families move to the Hauran after the 1860 war
why: Cuinet and Baedeker both say the Druze population of the Hauran rose sharply from 1861, giving the Jabal Hauran its later name Jabal al-Druze.
note: Second source: Baedeker 1894 (archive.org/details/baedekerspalesti0000karl).

title: European Commission holds its 25th and last Beirut meeting
why: Five months of sessions end without agreed punishments; the plan for governing Mount Lebanon passes to the ambassadors at Istanbul.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 209; Churchill 1862, p. 255-256

title: First Masonic lodge in Beirut founded under the Grand Lodge of Scotland
why: Wikipedia, citing a dictionary of Arab Freemasons, says Lodge Palestine No. 415 opened in May 1861; Butrus al-Bustani belonged to it around 1865.
note: Secondary and unverified against Scottish lodge records.

title: French troops begin embarking from Beirut by night
why: The 1860 expeditionary force leaves after about ten months; Churchill describes the first embarkation as stealthy, with the rest following openly.
note: Existing record gives month only; Churchill gives 5 June, Jessup gives 8 June for the last soldier.

title: Last French soldier sails from Beirut
why: Jessup puts the end of the French occupation at 8 June 1861, almost ten months after the August 1860 landing.

title: Règlement Art. 16 fixes the Mountain tax at 3,500 purses
why: Istanbul levies 3,500 purses (393,750 francs) through the governor, raisable to 7,000; local costs and public works come first.

title: Protocol sets governor title mushir, seat Deir al-Qamar, 3-year term
why: Aali Pasha adds that the Christian governor reports to the Porte, can be removed only after a judgment, and the Powers are consulted before renewal.

title: Règlement Art. 15: local police of seven men per thousand
why: Order is kept by volunteer gendarmes at seven per 1,000 inhabitants; Ottoman troops garrison the Beirut-Damascus and Saida-Tripoli roads meanwhile.
note: Art. 14 of the 1864 text repeats the 7-per-1,000 ratio.

title: Règlement Art. 2: central council of 12, two per community
why: The 1861 text gives the governor an advisory council of two Maronites, two Druze, two Greek Catholics, two Orthodox, two Metawali and two Sunnis.
dup_of: Administrative council of twelve set up under the Règlement

title: Règlement Art. 3: six administrative districts with local councils
why: Kourah, north Lebanon, Zahle, Matn, the area south of the Damascus road to Jezzine, and Jezzine-Tuffah each get an agent and a council of 3-6.

title: Règlement Arts. 7-10: village judges, two-tier courts, Beirut commercial court
why: Judges of the peace rule to 500 piastres; a 12-member higher council sits at the seat of government; commercial cases go to Beirut.

title: Règlement Art. 17 orders a census by commune and rite
why: The statute calls for a population count by commune and rite and a cadastre of cultivated land; the sources do not date its completion.
note: Wikipedia says Daud Pasha counted the population and surveyed land; no date given.

title: British midshipmen wreck a Beirut confectioner's shop and are court-martialled
why: Five men from HMS Mars did 5,000 francs of damage; Jessup says they were imprisoned and fined in full.

title: Daud Pasha inaugurated as governor of Mount Lebanon
why: Jessup dates the inauguration to 18 July 1861; Cuinet says only that he was named in July. Jessup dates the new regime to 10 June.
dup_of: Daoud Pasha nominated first mutasarrif of Mount Lebanon

title: Damascus indemnity collection sparks a thwarted plot against the pasha
why: Jessup says Ottoman officials began collecting about a million dollars from Damascus Muslims, who plotted to kill the pasha and remaining Christians.
note: Missionary hearsay, not checked against Ottoman or consular records. Month inferred from surrounding text.

title: English visitor defaces Napoleon III inscription at the Dog River tablets
why: A young Englishman named Lee chipped the emperor's name from a French plaque cut over an ancient tablet; the French consul complained and dropped it.
note: Month inferred; text places it after early August 1861 and before September.

title: American Board orders one-third spending cut; Syria mission closes boarding schools
why: The US Civil War squeezed donations; missionaries cut their own and native staff pay and shut the boarding schools.

title: Beirut hit by its first dengue epidemic
why: About 25,000 of roughly 60,000 residents fell ill; few died. Jessup blames refugee crowding and filth. It ended after rain around early December.
note: Year fixed by chapter sequence (French fleet leaves Oct 1861; Fuad Pasha prays for rain c. 1 Dec; he leaves 14 Dec 1861).

title: French fleet leaves Beirut; two Druze notables released from prison
why: Yusuf Abd al-Malik and Emir Muhammad Arslan, held after 1860, go home and later serve in the Lebanon government.

title: Fuad Pasha leaves Beirut to become Grand Vizier
why: The envoy behind the 1860-61 settlement sails on the frigate Tayif amid public farewells; Jessup calls him the most popular Ottoman in Syria.

title: Daud Pasha adopts more liberal policy toward Protestants
why: He names an Englishman chief of police and a Protestant, Naama Tabet, secretary, and orders cemeteries built in all Lebanon towns.
note: Jessup places this in the latter part of 1862.

title: Antoura college admissions reach about 200 pupils
why: Cuinet says the Lazarist college, begun in 1837 with 17 pupils and 60 in 1854, received nearly 200 by 1862.

title: Beirut receives three hairs of the Prophet from the Sultan
why: Troops with music and banners escort the relic to the Great Mosque; Jessup records mixed Muslim reactions, some doubting the relics.

title: Daniel Bliss sails to raise funds for a Beirut college
why: The Syria Mission voted in January 1862 to found the college; Bliss left for New York. Jessup gives 24 August, Bliss gives 14 August.
cite: Bliss 1920, p. 168; Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 240
note: Date conflict between the two memoirs (14 vs 24 Aug 1862); first is Bliss himself.

title: British commissioner Colonel Frazier resigns and leaves Syria
why: Jessup credits him with preventing several outbreaks of violence after 1860; the missionary says his health broke under constant work.

title: Beirut population put at 70,000, up from 22,000 in 1856
why: Jessup quotes 6,000 in 1823, 10,000 in 1840, 22,000 in 1856 and 70,000 in 1863; seven European steamer lines called at the port.
note: Missionary estimate, not a census; Jessup uses 60,000 for 1861. Official 1889 figure is 105,400 (Baedeker).

title: First telegram goes from Beirut to Constantinople
why: Jessup records the first telegraphic despatch on 1 February 1863 and quotes Moslem wonder at the wire.
dup_of: Beirut linked by telegraph to Istanbul
note: Existing record gives the year only.

title: Storm snows Lebanon and drives a French steamer ashore at Beirut
why: The Jourdan broke in two but every passenger was landed by a line; Tripoli and Sidon orange trees wore snow caps.
note: "All safely landed" per Jessup; ship crew not mentioned.

title: Daud Pasha addresses Lebanese notables at Easter reception
why: He tells the assembled notables that the governor, the people and tradition are the three parties in Lebanon and that cooperation defeats disorder.
note: Date taken from "Easter, 1863"; Easter fell on 5 April 1863 (calendar fact, not in source).

title: Beirut managers approve by-laws for the Syrian Protestant College
why: Meeting at Van Dyck's house adopts the by-laws sent from New York, insisting on the college's evangelical character.

title: Additional article: tax above 7,000 purses needs Porte and council consent
why: The 7,000-purse ceiling is not absolute; any rise above it needs Istanbul's authorisation and a majority of the central administrative council.
law_no: Additional article to Protocol of 9 June 1861
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1869, t. I, p. 217 (additional article to the 1861 protocol)
note: The print gives the signing date as 19 June 1864 (OCR); the main 1864 Règlement is dated 6 Sept 1864. Date treated as 1864 only.

title: New York governor signs bill incorporating Syrian Protestant College
why: Bliss says Governor Seymour signed the bill for the college and Robert College on 14 May 1864; trustees elected Bliss president on 14 July.
dup_of: New York State grants charter to Syrian Protestant College
note: CONFLICT: existing record dates the charter to 24 April 1863. Bliss (editor note) gives 14 May 1864 for the signed bill. Needs NY State Archives check.

title: Van Dyck reports the Arabic Old Testament translation finished
why: The Beirut press completes the Smith-Van Dyck Arabic Bible text; Jessup gives 22 August in one chapter and 23 August in another.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 150 and p. 218
note: Day differs inside Jessup (22 vs 23 Aug 1864).

title: 1864 statute: clergy tried by church courts; no sanctuary from prosecutors
why: Arts. 16-17 keep cases involving only clergy under ecclesiastical jurisdiction unless the bishop agrees, and bar church premises from sheltering suspects.

title: 1864 statute: council members elected by village sheikhs, renewed by thirds
why: Art. 10 has judges named by the governor and council members elected by sheikhs, with one third renewed every two years.
note: The 1861 text renewed half the council every year.

title: 1864 statute: council of 12 from seven districts, four Maronites
why: Delegates from the mudirates choose the council: Maronite 4, Druze 3, Orthodox 2, Greek Catholic 1, Sunni 1, Metawali 1.
dup_of: Revised Règlement Organique signed, making the statute permanent
note: Seat count computed from the delegation table in Art. 2; matches Wikipedia 4/3/2/1/1/1.

title: 1864 statute: three first-instance courts and village judges to 200 piastres
why: Village sheikhs judge up to 200 piastres (500 in 1861); three first-instance courts and a six-judge higher council replace the old mixed councils.

title: Professor Salisbury reads a translated Nusayri catechism to the American Oriental Society
why: The Arabic text came from Sulayman al-Adani, a convert who reached Beirut in November 1862; the translation appeared in the Society's journal in 1865.
note: Jessup says Salisbury read it on 18 May and 27 Oct 1864; Sulayman was later killed, per Jessup.

title: Paris urges consul to avoid force against Karam after his return
why: Drouyn de Lhuys calls Joseph Karam's return a regrettable event; he wants conciliation, with Karam submitting without reservation to Daud Pasha.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1866, t. I, p. 234 (dispatch to consul-general Outrey)
dup_of: Karam allowed back to Ehden; campaigns against the mutasarrifate
note: Existing record gives 1864 only.

title: France presses the Maronite patriarch to help calm Karam's return
why: A second dispatch welcomes Daud Pasha's plan to use only friendly means and says France would be grateful for the patriarch's efforts.

title: Orthodox notables persecute Protestants at Safita; Syria governor arrests leaders
why: Crops burned, houses attacked and a community driven out; Rashid Pasha, new governor of Syria, arrested the chief persecutors after an appeal.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 289 and p. 292

title: American mission launches the weekly al-Nashra al-Usbu'iyya
why: Jessup says the weekly paper had run 25 years in 1890 and predated the press laws by four years, putting its start about 1865.
note: Start year computed from "twenty-five years" and "four years before the 1869 laws"; not stated directly.

title: Daud Pasha resolves to resign; France asks Powers to defend statute
why: Drouyn de Lhuys cites the Porte's alarm and three years of relative calm; any successor should be chosen under the 1861 and 1864 texts.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1866, t. I, p. 235-236 (circular of 3 Mar 1865)
note: Moustier reported on 15 Feb 1865 that Ottoman ministers were pressing Daud to reconsider.

title: American Press celebrates printing of the complete Arabic Bible
why: A ceremony at the Beirut press marks the printed Old Testament; speakers included Butrus al-Bustani and Rev. James Robertson.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 150 and p. 283

title: Karam submits to Daud Pasha after an accord with the Maronite patriarch
why: French consul des Essarts reports the country quiet; Kesrawan villagers who had withheld tax now accept the principle and ask time to pay arrears.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1866, t. I, p. 236-237 (dispatches of 8 and 11 Apr 1865)
note: Telegram dated 1 April per Drouyn de Lhuys, 8 April; detailed report 11 April.

title: Van Dyck sails for New York to electrotype the Arabic Bible
why: He leaves with the finished text to cast plates for the American Bible Society; duplicates later go to New York, London and Beirut.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 153 and p. 283; vol. II, p. 812

title: Cholera from Egypt reaches Beirut; 20,000 flee and 3,000 die
why: Jessup saw crowds leave before the first local case; Lebanese villages imposed 15-day quarantines on Beirut. Locusts and cattle disease struck the same summer.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 283 and p. 288-289
note: Jessup estimates "not less than 3,000" deaths in Beirut, mostly Muslims; a missionary estimate, no official count. A fatwa allowed Muslims to flee (see vol. II, p. 446).

title: Sultan's order lets mission goods enter customs free of duty
why: Jessup received a copy of the order giving missionaries, clergy, rabbis and teachers the same privilege the French had; it was later curtailed.
note: Text says "the last of September, 1865".

title: Porte abandons 3-4 million piastres of Qaimaqamate-era tax arrears to the Mountain
why: The arrears are to fund public works; French officials expected villagers to pay them willingly if the money stayed local.

title: Porte promises an annual subsidy of 3 million piastres to Lebanon's budget
why: Because the Mountain's own revenue could not cover the gendarmerie and administration, Istanbul commits to a yearly grant to the governor.

title: Druze chiefs amnestied in 1865 may return only with the governor's permission
why: Daud Pasha stays sole judge of the terms for their return, after fearing the amnesty for those named in the 1860 killings could threaten order.

title: Cossack and Muslim squadrons to guard Damascus and Saida roads
why: Two Christian and two Muslim squadrons replace infantry on the roads the Règlement left under Ottoman guard.

title: Daud Pasha withdraws his second resignation after Porte concessions
why: After leave in Constantinople he again sought to quit, fearing the Druze amnesty; French lobbying won a package and the Porte lent a state ship.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1866, t. I, p. 237-238 (circular of 28 Sep 1865)

title: Part of the Bekaa plain moved from Damascus to Lebanon
why: The package detaches a district of the Bekaa, mainly inhabited by Lebanese, from the Damascus government and places it under the Lebanon governor.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1866, t. I, p. 238; also p. 171 (Règlement du Liban summary)
note: Cuinet 1896 lists Zahle with the seven Mountain cazas; the exact boundary change is not described in these sources.

title: Plan to raise a 1,500-man regulation gendarmerie in Lebanon
why: The concession package says the gendarmerie envisaged by the Règlement would be organised at 1,500 men; progress had been slow.

title: Porte grants annual subsidy to keep Daud Pasha in post
why: Moustier says Kesrawan's refusal to pay tax starved the budget for the gendarmerie; Istanbul added an allocation months before March 1866 to stop Daud resigning.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1867, t. I, p. 323-324 (Moustier to Drouyn de Lhuys, 21 Mar 1866)
note: Month inferred: the dispatch says "a few months ago" in March 1866. Treat the date as approximate (late 1865).

title: Kerosene lamp oil first imported into Syria
why: George Hurter brought a Boston cargo of kerosene and pine in autumn 1866; by 1870 it had largely replaced olive oil for lighting.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 313-315 and p. 361
note: Jessup p. 361 says 1865 for the introduction; p. 313 says autumn 1866.

title: Karam marches on Daud Pasha at Jounieh; Ghazir attacked twice
why: Consul des Essarts telegraphs that the sheikh attacked Ghazir on 6 January and was repulsed, and that the rising did not spread to mixed districts.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1866, t. I, p. 238 (telegram of 7 Jan 1866)

title: France gives Daud Pasha moral support against Karam
why: Drouyn de Lhuys tells the consul to assure Daud of France's backing for suppressing the revolt.

title: French ambassador reports Karam in open revolt, marching on Jounieh
why: Moustier writes that Karam leads about 1,000 men toward Jounieh, Daud Pasha's seat; he links the rising to Kesrawan's refusal of the regular tax.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1867, t. I, p. 320 (dispatch of 10 Jan 1866)

title: Kesrawan asks amnesty through clergy; Karam shelters in a convent
why: Des Essarts reports Daud Pasha willing to grant it and Karam sheltering near Batroun; Paris reads this as the failure of the venture.
note: Later fighting (Jan-Aug 1866) shows the telegram's optimism was premature.

title: Report says Karam has allied with Metawali chief Salman Harfush
why: A Tripoli deputy-governor telegram to the Grand Vizier, relayed by Moustier, names Salman Harfush, whom he calls a highway robber, as Karam's ally.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1867, t. I, p. 321 (dispatch of 17 Jan 1866)

title: Karam and Emir Salman al-Harfush attack Ghazir by land and sea
why: The Maronite leader and the Shiite emir of Baalbek, both stripped of power by the new order, coordinate an assault on the Kesrawan town.
cite: Wikipedia, Yusuf Karam (section on the 1866 revolt)
note: Secondary source; Wikipedia cites French consular dispatches of 5 Feb and 18 Mar 1866.

title: Moustier calls Karam an instrument of the Maronite patriarch
why: He argues the Kesrawan clergy, owners of most estates there, wanted to stay tax-exempt and resisted the Règlement.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1867, t. I, p. 321-322 (dispatch of 14 Feb 1866)
note: A French official reading; the patriarch's side is not given in the source.

title: France backs the Règlement and urges a mixed police force
why: Drouyn de Lhuys circular says the Karam rising does not alter the 1861 arrangement and that forming the gendarmerie has gone with extreme slowness.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1867, t. I, p. 322-323 (circular of 20 Feb 1866)

title: Locusts return; Beirut men ordered out to collect egg-bearing insects
why: Each man had to deliver six pounds; Jessup lists cholera, cattle murrain, civil war and locusts as successive plagues with heavy taxation.

title: French consul-general warns Harfush presence in Koura will delay submission
why: His report to Paris says the emir's return to the northern mountains complicates efforts to bring the rebels in without driving them to extremes.
cite: Wikipedia, Yusuf Karam (cites French consular dispatch of 18 Mar 1866)

title: Napoleon III refuses Karam hospitality in France
why: Moustier says the refusal pleased Aali Pasha; Daud Pasha had lacked a local armed force because Kesrawan withheld taxes and Istanbul refused conscription.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1867, t. I, p. 323-324 (dispatch of 21 Mar 1866)

title: Daud Pasha declares Harfush-Karam revolt over; troops to leave
why: He telegraphs that regular troops would start leaving next day and hold the Tripoli-Beirut road only provisionally.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1867, t. I, p. 324 (telegram relayed 28 Mar 1866)
note: Wikipedia lists Karam battles after this date (June-Aug 1866); the telegram describes the revolt as ended but fighting resumed.

title: Karam escapes encirclement near Baalbek and offers submission to Ottoman commander
why: He asks to withdraw to Rumelia with equivalent property; the Grand Vizier tells Dervish Pasha to refer to Daud Pasha and accept no conditions.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1867, t. I, p. 325-326 (dispatch of 4 Apr 1866)

title: Maronite patriarch visits Daud Pasha; Kesrawan tax collection to proceed
why: Moustier reports the call was returned and that Daud expects 500 gendarmes under arms within two months once the Kesrawan pays.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1867, t. I, p. 326-327 (dispatch of 11 Apr 1866)

title: Objection raised to a Syrian professor at the new Beirut college
why: When managers named John Wortabet to the medical chair, New York objected that he was not American; Thomson threatened to quit if natives were barred.

title: Leonid meteor shower alarms Beirut; muezzins call the faithful to prayer
why: A watchman at the Protestant College raised the alarm; Jessup says the common people were in terror. Showers fell on 12-14 November.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 316-317; vol. II, p. 499

title: Karam's men and government forces fight at Ehden
why: Wikipedia lists the Ehden engagement of 15 December 1866 among the last battles of the Karam revolt, before the January 1867 fights.
note: The article labels each fight a Lebanese victory; treat outcomes as one-sided.

title: Prussian Johanniter hospital inaugurated in Beirut
why: The Knights of St John hospital opens with German and Arabic addresses; the American college doctors took over its medical work in 1871.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 317; Cuinet 1896, p. 57

title: Karam revolt: fighting at Ejbeh and Aarjes
why: One of the final engagements before Karam's departure on a French ship on 31 January 1867.

title: Karam revolt: fighting at Wadi el-Salib
why: Wikipedia lists this as the last recorded clash before Karam accepted exile in Algeria.

title: Quaker City excursion steamer, with Mark Twain aboard, reaches Beirut
why: Jessup arranged a dragoman for a party to Baalbek and Damascus, and gave each passenger an Arabic New Testament.

title: Van Dyck returns with Arabic Bible plates and an electrotyper
why: Samuel Hallock came with him to run the press; Americans also brought the first steam press to Syria in 1867, Jessup says.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 334 and p. 361

title: Ophthalmia epidemic fills new college dispensary in Beirut
why: Van Dyck wrote in 1869 that most patients at the dispensary opened that month were suffering from the autumn epidemic; a small hospital followed.
cite: SPC Annual Reports, report for 1868-69 (letter of Van Dyck, 6 Feb 1869)

title: Daud Pasha era: 8.5 km of road built in seven years
why: Cuinet counts 8.5 km under Daud Pasha for 170,000 piastres; the first governor had been Istanbul's former public works minister.

title: St George's School for Muslim and Druze girls opens in Beirut
why: Miss Jessie Taylor, a Scottish teacher working in the Bashura quarter since 1866, opens the school; by 1869 she had 75 Muslim pupils.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 232 and p. 315-316

title: Protocol accepts Daud Pasha's resignation; Fuad Pasha pledges Franco ten years
why: Signed at Kanlidja by the Porte and the Powers; Fuad says Nasri Franco Pasha's term will not be shorter than ten years from appointment.
cite: Noradounghian 1900, vol. III, no. 778, p. 278; Cuinet 1896, p. 207
dup_of: Daoud Pasha resigns; Franko Pasha becomes mutasarrif
note: Primary text of the protocol; supersedes the secondary Cuinet citation in the 1868 record above.

title: Suez Canal opening diverts trade away from Syrian ports
why: Hitti says the canal sidetracked world traffic from Syria and dealt Syrian traders a heavy blow, one cause of later emigration.
note: Hitti 1924 is a historian's retrospective; the opening date of 17 Nov 1869 comes from general knowledge, not this page.

title: Ottoman press and school laws promulgated
why: Jessup says the 1869 laws, not translated into Arabic for years, required an imperial permit for periodicals and set up state schooling.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 433, p. 549 and p. 811
note: Press permit rules in the Ottoman Empire are usually traced to the 1864 press regulation; Jessup states 1869 and this record follows him.

title: Ismail al-Atrash, Druze chief of the Hauran, dies
why: Cuinet and Baedeker both name him as the leading Druze sheikh of the Hauran, where many Lebanese Druze had settled after 1860.

title: Beirut Evangelical Church building dedicated
why: Jessup preached the Arabic sermon at 9 a.m.; the church also served the English-language Anglo-American congregation.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 331 and p. 346-347

title: American theological class opens at Abeih
why: Calhoun, Eddy and Jessup teach a summer class for Syrian pastors; the class moved to Beirut in 1873.
note: Appendix V (vol. II, p. 811) dates the Abeih seminary to May 1868; the chapter text says 3 May 1869.

title: Mrs Bowen Thompson, founder of the British Syrian Schools, dies
why: Twelve years of work left 23 schools, 1,522 pupils and 79 teachers; her sisters continued the schools, reaching 40 schools and 3,000 pupils.

title: Drought and near famine in Syria; flour reaches $12.50 a barrel
why: Jessup reports deaths from hunger near Mount Carmel and a war scare that sent Damascus Christians preparing to flee to Beirut.
dup_of: Silk harvest falls below one third of normal

title: Beirut military hospital of 200 beds added to the barracks
why: Cuinet dates it to about 1870; by the mid-1890s Beirut also had French and Prussian hospitals of 100 beds each and a 50-bed Russian one.
note: "Vers 1870" in the source.

title: Hadiqat al-Akhbar starts a French edition
why: The Beirut weekly founded in 1858 begins appearing in Arabic and French from 1870, as Journal de Syrie et Liban.
note: Cuinet 1896, p. 58 lists the official Journal de Syrie et Liban as the oldest of 12 Beirut papers in the mid-1890s.

title: Syria Mission passes from the American Board to the Presbyterian Board
why: Reunification of US Presbyterians moved the Beirut mission and its press to the new Board; Jessup was offered its New York secretaryship and declined.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 371-375 and vol. II, p. 812

title: Syrian Protestant College graduates its first class
why: The class of 1870 was small; Bliss wrote that it included a future leading physician of Palestine and a future Arabic editor.
cite: Bliss 1920, p. 51; Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 304
note: The medical department's first class graduated in 1871 (Jessup).

title: Alexander Duff dedicates Scottish mission schools at Suk el-Gharb
why: The Lebanon Schools Committee of the Free Church built stone school buildings; a title dispute over the site began in 1872.

title: Istanbul refuses to authorise Syrian Protestant College medical diplomas
why: Bliss spent the summer in Constantinople seeking permission to grant degrees that the government would recognise; the effort failed.

title: College faculty and Prussian hospital agree terms for clinical teaching
why: The Curatorium and Van Dyck draft seven articles: the faculty staffs the hospital free and may use it for supervised student visits; Berlin must ratify.
cite: SPC Annual Reports, report for 1870-71 (minutes of 13 June 1871)
note: The order's letter of 16 March 1871 set the conditions.

title: William E. Dodge lays the cornerstone of College Hall in Beirut
why: Bliss says the college welcomes every class and creed; Jessup says its iron beams and flat stone arches were a first in Syria.
cite: Bliss 1920, p. 198; Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 412

title: Suk el-Gharb school title dispute begins: Scots mission v. superintendent
why: The Scottish committee had built on land owned by its Syrian superintendent, who kept the keys; litigation ran about fifteen years.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 383-384; vol. II, p. 520
note: Under Ottoman law buildings went with the land; the superintendent is not named in the source.

title: Mount Lebanon cocoon crop peaks at 5 million oqqa
why: Cuinet says output was far higher than in his day; a silkworm epidemic later forced the switch to imported Japanese seed.
note: An oqqa is roughly 1.28 kg; the source gives the figure in oqqas only.

title: Druze expectation that Hakim would return in 1872 goes unmet
why: Jessup wrote that some Druze said they would turn Muslim or Protestant if the prophecy failed; he reports a leading man saying so.

title: Zahle becomes a Presbyterian mission station; church organised in June 1873
why: Gerald Dale arrives in November 1872 to run the new station; the Zahle church building was dedicated in November 1876.

title: Franco Pasha era: 17.75 km of road, mostly by corvée
why: Only 3 km were paid for, at 62,000 piastres; the rest was built by forced labour, which Cuinet says Turkey had long abolished.

title: Franco Pasha dies in office; buried at Hazmieh
why: The 22 April 1873 protocol cites his death as the vacancy; Baedeker later notes his tomb at Hazmiyeh near Beirut.
cite: Noradounghian 1900, vol. III, p. 346; Baedeker 1894, p. 288
note: Exact death date not given in these sources, only that it precedes 22 April 1873.

title: Syrian Protestant College moves to its Ras Beirut campus
why: Bliss says the college left its rented third house in 1873; Jessup records iron beams and stone arches used for the first time in Syria.
cite: Bliss 1920, p. 188; Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 412

title: Protocol names Rustem Pasha governor after Franco Pasha's death
why: Porte and six Powers agree the appointment of the former Istanbul ambassador to St Petersburg; the ten-year term of the 1868 protocol is confirmed.
cite: Noradounghian 1900, vol. III, no. 815, p. 346; Cuinet 1896, p. 295
note: Cuinet p. 207 lists Rustem as appointed 22 July 1873 and Jessup dates his arrival to May 1873; the protocol itself is dated 22 April.

title: Rustem Pasha arrives to govern Lebanon
why: Jessup calls him the ablest governor Lebanon had known: he curbed bribery, imposed sanitary rules and kept the Maronite hierarchy in check.
dup_of: Rustem Pasha raises taxes, opens schools and roads; dispute with archbishop
note: Jessup heading says May 1873; Cuinet p. 207 gives 22 July 1873 for the appointment. Date uncertain by up to two months.

title: Beirut water company engineers and Daniel Bliss explore the Jeita caves
why: Maxwell and Huxley, building the Dog River aqueduct, pushed boats into the cave; a second trip in 1874 reached 1,060 metres.
cite: Thomson 1886, The Land and the Book (Lebanon vol.), p. 99-100; Bliss 1920, p. 242; Wikipedia, Jeita Grotto
note: Thomson calls them the Dog River caves; Wikipedia identifies the system as Jeita.

title: Fevers lay low tens of thousands from Gaza to Aleppo
why: Jessup wrote in September that 150 of 600 people in Ain Zehalteh were ill; Turkish troops sent against Moab tribes fell sick.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 437-438 (letter of 19 Sep 1874)
note: Letter-writer's estimate, no mortality data.

title: Zahle officials banish a mission bookseller; accusing priest later banished
why: Jessup says Rev. Gerald Dale was troubled by the arbitrary arrest; the priest who made the complaint was banished after striking the same helper.

title: Storms and snow block the Damascus road for two weeks
why: Jessup describes landslides, floods and roofs collapsing in Lebanon villages after a winter of drought and then deluge.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 434-435 (letter of 12 Feb 1874)

title: Mission weighs closing al-Nashra because of funding crisis
why: Jessup wrote that cuts were forcing the American mission to reduce printing, shut some schools and consider stopping its Arabic weekly.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 435 (letter of 12 Feb 1874)
note: The paper survived until its 1890 suspension.

title: Imperial firman raises Rustem Pasha to vizier and governor-general of Lebanon
why: The text tells him to uphold the organic regulations and promises he will be kept in post while he governs under them.
cite: Cuinet 1896, p. 296-297 (Annexe 4); Noradounghian 1900, vol. III, p. 346-347
note: Cuinet converts 15 Dhu al-Hijja 1290 to 3 February 1874; Noradounghian prints the same text under the 22 April 1873 protocol.

title: George Fisher takes up the American consulate in Beirut
why: His 1879 pamphlet says missionaries opposed his posting; his later dismissal of three dragomans sparked a public protest.
note: Partisan self-published account by the consul; page numbers approximate (OCR). Treat claims as one side.

title: American residents meet in Beirut to protest the consul's dismissal of dragomans
why: Missionaries and others sign a call after Fisher replaces three honorary dragomans; the consul complains of a campaign against him.
note: Partisan source; other side not read.

title: Dog River water reaches Beirut; celebration held at the upper reservoir
why: Attended by the Governor of Syria, the Lebanon governor, the pasha of Beirut and Abd el-Kader; Baedeker later credits the Beirut Water Works Company.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 441; Baedeker 1894, p. 286
dup_of: Beirut gets a water distribution company
note: Cuinet p. 56 says regular supply began in 1876 under the Beirut Water Works Company.

title: Cholera reaches Saghbin near Zahle; Gerald Dale treats the sick
why: Priests and villagers fled to the vineyards; Dale used a laudanum, camphor and rhubarb remedy and Jessup says only one patient died afterwards.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 443-444 and p. 500
note: Only one death after Dale arrived; earlier toll not stated.

title: Beirut Muslim weekly Thamarat al-Funun urges Muslims to stay put during cholera
why: Its editor Sheikh Ibrahim al-Ahdab argued that fate fixes the hour of death while many Muslims were leaving for the mountains.
note: Jessup calls the paper "new"; the Society of Arts launched it on 20 April 1875 (existing record).

title: Cholera reaches Beirut; Lebanon imposes a six-day quarantine
why: About 20,000 residents fled to the mountain; the city cleaned streets and a Muslim journal urged calm under fate.

title: Jesuit university transferred from Ghazir to Beirut
why: Cuinet says Saint-Joseph, founded at Ghazir in 1842, moved to Beirut in 1876, where it ran a university and a medical-pharmacy faculty.
dup_of: Jesuit seminary moves from Ghazir to Beirut and becomes Saint Joseph University
note: CONFLICT: existing record says 1875.

title: Missionary says the Syrian "discovered America" at the Centennial Exposition
why: Rev. O. J. Hardin dated the start of mass emigration to 1876; Jessup adds about one-twentieth of Syria's people had left by 1909.
note: Retrospective remark; 1909 emigrant share is Jessup's own estimate.

title: Abdulhamid II becomes Sultan
why: Jessup records the accession date; it ends the Abdulaziz era that saw the Règlement, Karam revolt and Beirut's growth.

title: Circassians deported from Bulgaria settle in Syria
why: Jessup's appendix lists the 1877-78 "great Circassian deportation" among the period's events.

title: Muslim benevolent society opens girls' schools in Beirut and other cities
why: Jessup's appendix credits a "Mohammedan Society of Benevolent Intentions" with girls' schools in Beirut, Damascus, Tripoli and Aleppo.
note: Likely the Maqasid society; its usual founding date is 1878, not checked here.

title: Russia declares war on Turkey; 60,000 Syrian men taken for the army
why: Jessup says families were left destitute, new money taxes were levied and Christians feared reprisals.

title: First Syrian family reaches the United States
why: Hitti says Joseph Arbeely of Damascus arrived in 1878; a larger wave from Zahle followed in the early 1880s.

title: Beirut municipal election: 820 Christian and 440 Muslim voters
why: Jessup notes the Ottoman governor is ex officio president and could send municipal funds to Istanbul despite a Christian electoral majority.
note: Date from surrounding text (winter 1880); the exact poll date is not given.

title: French officer reportedly seeks Metawali and Nusayri petition for French protection
why: The Fortnightly Review alleged in 1883 that Major de Torcy, dressed as an Ottoman marshal, sounded out about 400,000 Metawali and Nusayris three years earlier.
note: Allegation in a British periodical hostile to French policy; no French source checked. Year derived from "three years ago".

title: Saint-Louis college opens at Ghazir under Maronite chorbishop Louis Zouain
why: Cuinet says it teaches in Arabic and French with ten professors and charged about 200 francs a year for boarding.
note: Source says October 1880.

title: Syrian Protestant College arts class taught entirely in English
why: Bliss and Jessup say the class of 1880 was the first fully instructed in English; medicine followed with the class of 1887.
cite: Bliss 1920, p. 216; Jessup 1910, vol. I, p. 304-305
note: Wikipedia (AUB) gives 1887 as the year English became the language of instruction.

title: Severe winter: wolves kill a priest caught in a Kesrawan storm
why: Jessup records the death in a winter he calls severe; the same page records the Beirut municipal election of 1880.

title: Officials force Dr Charles Calhoun out of Tripoli after a rival's intrigue
why: Samuel Jessup recalled that the missionary doctor, whose practice had grown, left in 1882, then won an imperial diploma to practise anywhere in the empire.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 460 and p. 482-483
note: Calhoun died at Shwifat on 22 June 1883 (same pages).

title: Rustem Pasha's ten years: 50.5 km of road built
why: The roads cost 989,500 piastres; Cuinet says the first three governors built 76 km in 22 years without a public works service.

title: Wassa Pasha builds Baabda and Beiteddine offices, qonaqs and village water lines
why: Cuinet lists Baabda palace, qonaqs at Zahle, Jezzine, Jounieh, Batroun and Kourah, a Beiteddine hospital and pipes at Baaqlin (4.5 km) and Damour (7 km).
dup_of: Wasa Pasha builds Beiteddine hospital and Baabda and Zahle seraglios
note: Source dates the programme 1883-91; the existing record gives 1883.

title: Wassa Pasha creates a roads service and in-kind labour with cash buy-out
why: Cuinet says 30 of the 76 km built earlier were redone; by 1891-92 he delivered 131 km at 2.28 million piastres.
note: Source dates the 131 km programme 1883 to 1891-92, beyond this file's span.

title: A British review counts 200,000 Maronites and 82 convents
why: The Fortnightly Review puts the Maronite clergy's revenue at about 70,000 pounds a year and says Rustem Pasha curbed deathbed bequests.
note: Unsourced figures in an opinion article; a sympathetic view of Rustem Pasha.

title: French medical faculty opens at Saint-Joseph University, urged by Leo XIII
why: Cuinet says the faculty, subsidised by France, had ten professors and 64 external students by the mid-1890s; Paris examiners gave the doctorate.

title: Rustem Pasha's term expires; France threatens to break relations if he stays
why: The Fortnightly Review says Ambassador de Noailles gave the Porte this deadline, but Rustem stayed until 6 June while the Powers argued over a successor.
note: British periodical commentary hostile to France; the threat is not checked against French records.

title: Porte sets aside France's candidate Nasri Bey and nominates Wassa Pasha
why: The review says Nasri Bey was rejected as clerical and incompetent; a German, Strecker Pasha, was floated before the Powers accepted Wassa.
note: Month approximate; the formal protocol is dated 8 May.

title: Protocol appoints Wassa Pasha governor of Lebanon
why: Signed in Constantinople by the six Powers and the Porte; the former Edirne official's term is set under the ten-year rule of 1868 and 1873.
cite: Noradounghian 1902, vol. IV, no. 920, p. 314; Cuinet 1896, p. 297-298

title: Wassa Pasha lands at Beirut to a French frigate's 21-gun salute
why: He tells Druze, Metawali, Orthodox and Maronite deputations he will follow the Règlement and govern himself.
note: The Porte kept Rustem Pasha in post until this date, per the same article.

title: Imperial firman installing Wassa Pasha read at Hadath
why: The reading took place at the governor's winter residence on 7/19 June; the firman names him vizier and governor-general of Lebanon in Rustem Pasha's place.
cite: Archives diplomatiques 1882-83, 2nd series, t. VIII, p. 94-95
note: Fortnightly Review has Wassa landing at Beirut on 6 June; the firman itself is dated 3 Rajab 1300.

title: Russia hands the Porte a note listing four infringements of the Règlement
why: The Fortnightly Review reads it as a reminder of Russia's interest as protector of the Orthodox, one complaint being favouritism toward Maronites.
note: Month inferred: note "just been handed" in the 1 Sept issue.

title: Salim al-Bustani dies; brother Najib continues the Arabic encyclopedia
why: Jessup says tight censorship, including two manuscript copies sent to Constantinople, stopped the Da'irat al-Ma'arif after ten volumes.
note: The month is "September, 1884" in the source.

title: Small salt works on the Latakia and Tripoli coast shut and destroyed
why: Cuinet says costs of extraction and guarding exceeded the price of salt brought from the large Phocée pans; date given as 1885 or 1886.
note: Source says "1885 ou 1886".

title: Syrian emigration swells between 1885 and the 1893 Chicago exposition
why: Hitti says the Zahle-led movement of the early 1880s spread across the eastern US and reached the Pacific coast before the 1890s surge.

title: Arriving missionaries spend six days in Beirut quarantine
why: Gerald Dale and others disembarked into the quarantine station; Jessup says European cholera had also forced a Black Sea detour that year.
cite: Jessup 1910, vol. II, p. 494 and p. 498

title: US consul Bissinger reports the Turkish takhmis method nearly doubled the tithe
why: Hitti cites the report as part of the economic background to Syrian emigration, alongside silk price pressure and later phylloxera.

title: Scottish mission wins Suk el-Gharb title case; property passes to Dr Carslaw
why: Jessup says the long suit was decided in 1887 and deeds and school furniture handed over; the property was then sold to the American mission.
note: Jessup p. 384 says sold in 1888; p. 521 says March 1889.

title: Mount Lebanon cocoon crop falls to 1.9 million oqqa
why: Cuinet contrasts 1887 with 5 million in 1872; the crop recovered to 2.9 million oqqa in 1888 after Japanese silkworm seed replaced local stock.

title: Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq dies near Istanbul; buried in Lebanon on 5 October
why: The Lebanese-born writer, founder of the Constantinople paper al-Jawa'ib (1861-84), is buried near Beirut; Baedeker later notes his tomb at Hazmiyeh.
cite: Wikipedia, Ahmad Faris al-Shidyaq; Baedeker 1894, p. 288
note: Wikipedia gives 20 Sep (death) and 5 Oct 1887 (burial in Lebanon).

title: Beirut port handles 2,767 sailing ships and 494 steamers
why: Baedeker reports 45,846 tons in sail and 501,368 tons in steam, and says Beirut's importance lies in imports; silk exports 2,600 bales.

title: Beirut streets lit by gas from a French company
why: Cuinet counts 656 public lamps and an ice plant; Baedeker also dates gas to 1888 and water to 1875, both from foreign companies.
note: CONFLICT: existing record gives 1887.

title: Beirut becomes a first-class vilayet separate from Syria
why: Cuinet says it reported directly to the Interior Ministry, split by Mount Lebanon; by the mid-1890s five sanjaks, 21 cazas, 2,237 villages.
dup_of: Beirut made capital of a new vilayet
note: Cuinet lists Beirut, Acre, Tripoli, Latakia and Balqa (Nablus); Wikipedia (History of Beirut) names Bekaa instead of Nablus. Structure shown is c. 1895.

title: US minister Oscar Straus visits Beirut
why: Jessup says the minister to Turkey, who defended American mission rights, impressed all who met him.

title: US consul reports Syrian cocoon deficit of 25 percent
why: Hitti quotes Bissinger: 5,626,697 pounds of cocoons produced, and local firms eager to ship silk directly to the United States.

title: French company starts construction of Beirut harbour
why: Baedeker says the new harbour would be the only safe anchorage between Port Said and Alexandria; it opened in 1894.
dup_of: Beirut port concession granted to French company
note: Source says "summer of 1889". CONFLICT: Cuinet p. 56-57 says works began in 1882; Wikipedia says the concession was granted in 1887.

title: Beirut official population: 105,400, led by Muslims then Greek Orthodox
why: Baedeker quotes 33,000 Muslims, 30,000 Greek Orthodox, 28,000 Maronites, 9,000 Melkites, 1,500 Jews and 1,500 Latins; Beirut had about 20,000 before 1860.
note: "Official statistics for 1889" per Baedeker; not an independent census.

title: France sends an agent to inspect the decaying Khan al-Franj at Sidon
why: Cuinet says the property, built up against by neighbours, risked ruin; a French credit followed in 1891 and restoration finished about late 1893.

title: Scottish committee sells Suk el-Gharb schools to the American mission
why: The sale ends a long dispute over title that began in 1872; the Presbyterian mission later opened a boys' boarding school on the site.
note: Jessup vol. I, p. 384 says 1888.

title: Two hairs of the Prophet's beard reach a Tripoli mosque
why: Jessup contrasts the reception with the three hairs sent to Beirut in 1862, which some Muslims there had ridiculed.

title: Beirut censor suspends the American mission weekly al-Nashra
why: The Beirut press officer bars the 25-year-old paper for lacking an imperial permit; Jessup petitions and the dispute runs through January.
note: Jessup names the governor as Aziz Pasha; the paper began in about 1865 by his own count.

title: First Greek Catholic priest sent to the US arrives in New York
why: Hitti says Abraham Bechawate of Zahle celebrated mass on Christmas Day in a church basement; Maronite priests had visited only to raise funds.
